content.thinking:
I'm planning the overall design for an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike with a teal body, orange accents, and steel details, working out realistic proportions like overall length, height, wheel sizes, and wheelbase before building it out.

Now I'm structuring the skeleton with a root frame joint and child joints for the front wheel, rear wheel, steering fork, swingarm, and handlebar, using hinge roles for articulation, while keeping geometry construction simple with boxes, cylinders, and rods tied to explicit bones and positions to avoid errors. I'm defining the wheel parts and tire geometry using a torus shape aligned along the x-axis.

Writing wheel spoke geometry...

For the aesthetic I'm going Overwatch-inspired: bold clean shapes with beveled edges and panel lines, a navy/teal body with a single orange accent, considering cel-style toon shading for that painted, stylized look.

Defining the paint functions for the tank's diagonal orange stripe pattern...

I'm reconsidering whether to add decal elements -- avoiding anything logo-like, so I'm exploring an abstract chevron shape as a textured plane positioned against the tank's ellipsoid surface, figuring out where the plane would sit relative to the scaled sphere geometry.

Then I'm sketching the bike's actual measurements: ground plane at y=0, front and rear wheel torus dimensions (radius and tube thickness) to get the right outer wheel sizes, setting the rear tire fatter and wider than the front for that chopper look, and placing their centers in 3D space accordingly.

Now I'm working out the front fork geometry, figuring the rake angle by computing the vector from the steering head down to the front axle, adjusting the axle's z-position until I get roughly a 40° rake typical of a chopper.

I'm placing the fork joints and tubes along that angled direction, with a steering joint at the head that the handlebars and headlight will inherit motion from, and starting the main frame backbone, running a rigid spine from the head back toward the seat area in true hardtail chopper style.

Next I'm routing the downtube and lower rail to the rear axle, then building the V-twin engine block near the frame's center — a crankcase box with two finned cylinders angled front-and-back in a V, each cylinder built from stacked thin fin discs along a tilted axis.

I'm setting up a general orientation helper that rotates geometry to align with an arbitrary direction vector, then using it to place the fin boxes along each cylinder's tilted axis. Now I'm shaping the fuel tank as a teardrop form sitting above the frame spine.

Then I'm working through the geometry of the steering head and fork angle, repositioning the tank so it doesn't collide with the fork neck, and calculating the fork tilt (~39.5°) so the axle lines up correctly with the steering head position.

For the sphere I'm deciding to use smoother segments (16x12) for a cleaner Overwatch-style look rather than a flat low-poly bevel. For the seat, I'm planning to build it as an extruded profile swept along the Z axis with bevel edges, defining a quilted outline of points to form the padded shape.

I'm now checking the geometry overlap between the seat, rear fender, and rear wheel -- the seat's rear extends close to where the wheel top sits, so I need to raise the seat's bottom edge slightly to clear the fender and wheel properly.

Finishing the seat outline, I'll close it with a smoothing bevel for the frame. Now I'm building the frame spine as a curved rod from the head to the rear, then adding seat rails and hardtail struts as swept paths.

For the rear structure I'm placing axle positions and wheel-strut widths relative to the tire width, then setting up the joint hierarchy: a root frame joint, steering joint, front and rear wheel joints as children, plus a kickstand hinge.

I'm deciding to keep lever controls minimal—clutch and brake levers as hinges—and confirming the bone/joint creation pattern where each part specifies its parent, position, and direction, always passing a bone reference for rigid attachment. Now I'm working out exhaust pipe routing along the right side of the engine toward the cylinder exhaust port.

I'm placing the exhaust as a curved sweep from near the engine down to the rear of the bike, ending in a chrome tip, with a perforated heat shield detail. Weighing which side should get the exhaust versus the drive chain based on the reference image, I'm settling on exhaust on the right and chain/kick pedal on the left.

Now I'm working out the foot controls, placing footpegs symmetrically with rubber grips positioned forward, then building the engine block as a crankcase box with round primary covers on each side, and settling on a steel and teal color palette for the body parts.

I'm figuring out the headlight placement relative to the fork tubes, computing the fork's directional vector to position the headlight correctly in front of it while staying within the color count limit.

Adding the headlight bezel ring, lens, and shell geometry, then starting to plan the ape hanger handlebar path with riser points sweeping up and out from the clamp.

Finishing the grip geometry and planning mirrors with faceted diamond stems, plus fork details: chrome upper tubes, navy lower sliders with orange bands, boots, teal T-tree plates with bolts, and a swept arc fender over the front wheel.

Working out the rear fender geometry too, sweeping from front-top to rear-down around the wheel center with a wider radius, keeping teal color with an orange stripe accent to match the front.

Now adding a small red taillight glow sphere near the fender's trailing edge, plus tiny amber turn-signal glow spheres mounted on short stalks. For the license plate, I'll skip real text/logos and instead compose a decorative plate graphic with simple rectangles facing backward.

I'm also adding a small instrument gauge cylinder at the handlebar clamp. For tire tread, I'm generating repeated tread blocks around each tire's circumference, orienting each block radially outward so it sits flush against the tire surface with a slight tangential width.

To get consistent orientation, I need a proper basis builder instead of relying on arbitrary rotation after aligning to the radial direction — so I'm writing a helper that constructs a full basis matrix (x, y, z axes) given a position, a y-direction (radial), and an x-hint, computing z as the cross product to keep the tangential axis aligned, then applying that transform to the geometry.

Now I'm working out tire tread block placement around the torus — sizing and spacing blocks on the outer radius for front and rear tires, and considering how to add a thin sidewall accent ring, possibly using an open cylinder geometry visible only from the outside.

For the sidewall stripe, I'm positioning a thin orange torus at the correct offset to sit flush against the tire sidewall without clipping through. For the rim, I'm planning a chrome torus for the wire wheel, a cylindrical hub, and a thin disc brake on one side.

I'm simplifying the brake disc by using a solid cylinder with a ring of small dark cylinders arranged around it to fake bolt holes, rather than trying to cut real geometry. For spokes, I'm planning around 36 thin cylinders crossing from the hub flange to the rim at offset angles to mimic a wire-wheel pattern cheaply.

Now I'm positioning the drivetrain: front and rear sprockets as cylinders at specific coordinates with different radii, connected by two thin dark steel rods standing in for the top and bottom chain runs, plus accounting for the primary cover on the engine's left side.

Then I'm placing the main engine components -- crankcase box, transmission housing behind it, and the front cylinder angled forward from the base at a set direction and length.

Adding cylinder fins, head, and air cleaner details...

Now adding a battery box with teal and orange styling on the opposite side plus a small tool box, then working out footboard pegs and the kickstand geometry—positioning the pivot joint and foot pad so it rests just above the floor while folded against the frame.

Checking tire contact points and tread blocks against the floor plane to make sure nothing clips more than a couple millimeters, and confirming the bike's overall height comes out around 1.35 units with mirrors reaching roughly 1.45.

Now I'm working out the paint logic for the body: defining a function that paints orange chevron stripes diagonally across the tank sides based on surface normal and position, plus a thin orange spine stripe running down the center top.

Adding dark navy countershading...

Adding diamond stitch pattern logic...

I'm thinking about adding decal textures via SVG for details like chevron stripes on battery/tool boxes and a speedo gauge face with ticks, generated as small canvas textures placed on flat panels.

For glow effects on the headlight lens, tail lamp, and signals, I need to check that the glow helper only applies to flat-colored materials rather than painted ones, since merged geometries only support flat color strings anyway. Now I'm sketching out helper functions to handle this merging and glow logic.

Writing basis-alignment helper...

Defining more part helpers...

Defining more joints...

Working out the lever rod geometry and joint directions for both grips, then planning a reusable wheel builder function with parameters for tire radius, tube thickness, and width.

Writing wheel geometry code...

Still computing tread geometry...

Still working out rim and hub geometry...

Now I'm adding the disc brake and sprocket as separate parts, keeping the wire-wheel spoke lengths consistent for the rear hub, then positioning the front brake disc on the fork with punched holes for a lightweight steel look.

I'm placing the caliper mount orange box behind the disc, aligned to the fork slider's incline so it sits correctly relative to the hub, and skipping the rear-right disc detail while adding the rear sprocket on the left.

Now I'm working out the fork geometry: the tube line runs from the steering joint through to the axle point, keeping the offsets consistent, with the upper chrome tube and lower slider following that same directional vector at different radius and length segments.

I'm defining the lower slider as navy-colored with an orange accent band partway down, plus chrome boots and axle cap details, then building the rod geometry using a bone-based rod function that takes start/end points, radius, color, and options. I'm also placing the triple tree plates—an upper teal box at the steering head and a lower tree box further down the fork line—sized and positioned to match the bike's steering geometry.

I'm working out the steering stem connection between the trees, positioning the frame's head tube as a separate navy cylinder on the frame bone rather than the steer bone, and adding handlebar riser clamps as small boxes on the steer assembly. Now I'm calculating the fork's tilt angle from vertical (about 39.5°) so I can rotate the tree plate boxes about the X-axis to align their orientation with the raked fork rather than sitting straight up.

I'm checking that the headlight placed between the fork tubes clears their surfaces at that height, and confirming the head tube and handlebar sweep geometry line up with the pivoting fork. Now I'm moving on to work out the front fender's curve, placing points around the wheel's center with a given radius and sweeping through an angle range.

I'm finding the fender overlaps slightly with the fork tubes' inner edges, so I'm narrowing the fender's width so it fits cleanly between the legs without clipping into them, while keeping clearance over the tire.

I'm setting the fender to follow the steering motion, built from a curved path with teal paint, an orange center stripe along the top face, and navy trim along the edges.

Now I'm adding chrome stay rods connecting the axle to the fender, then building the rear fender geometry as a similar curved band with its own struts, plus tail lamp glow, plate bracket, and turn signals. I'm sizing the rear fender radius to clear the wider rear tire, and starting the exhaust sweep path on the right side with negative x coordinates.

Still working out the exhaust path...

Still writing muffler geometry...

Building out the pipe geometry using catmull-smoothed paths with rigid bone attachments, then thinking through whether to add a second staggered exhaust pipe for the rear cylinder, sketching rough coordinates for where that rear exhaust path would exit the back face.

I'll skip the heat shield detail but add small torus bands for chrome rings along the pipes, then move to blocking out the footpeg geometry with steel rods and rubber inserts for right and left sides.

Checking the footpeg placement against the exhaust pipe path to avoid overlap, I'm positioning the right peg lower to clear the pipe, then adding a pivot box clamping onto the frame as a cradle plate mount before mirroring the setup for the left peg.

Now I'm placing the shift pedal on the left side: a shifter joint with a lever rod running upward to a ball end and rubber pad, positioned to avoid colliding with the forward peg by adjusting its height and offset.

Then I'm moving on to the lower frame cradle — plotting the downtube curve from the headstock down toward the engine cradle, adding rear lower rails and upper stays connecting the swingarm pivot area to the frame, and sketching the spine curve down the bike's backbone, all with specific coordinates and tube radii for a teal-painted frame.

I'm checking for collisions between the engine heads and the fuel tank — the cylinder heads poke up near where the tank sits, so I'm raising the tank's center position and adjusting its scale so the frame spine can pass cleanly through the V-gap between the cylinders.

Now I'm checking how the seat and tank overlap at the back, and that looks acceptable for a typical bike silhouette. For tank details, I'm placing a chrome filler cap with an orange ring on top of the tank surface.

Adding knee pads and edge strip...

Now I'm defining the tank paint function with conditions for navy belly below y=0.90, orange ridge stripe near the top edge, and side chevron patterns based on normal direction, using precomputed tone constants for each color region.

Next I'm setting up the seat geometry, extruding the outline along the bone frame with bevel and smoothing applied, and assigning the seat's color/paint.

Now I'm sketching a chrome sissy bar sweeping up from the rear frame in a curved loop, checking that its path clears the fender and rear tire, then planning to add a backrest pad.

I'm positioning the battery and tool boxes on either side of the rear frame, sizing them small and checking their placement against the transmission and rear wheel to avoid overlap.

Now I'm checking the chain path between the front and rear sprockets, confirming the y-coordinates so the chain line doesn't clip through the side boxes, and nudging the box height up near the seat bottom to clear it.

I realize the rear tire actually bulges out further than I thought at that height, overlapping the box bottom, so I need to shift the boxes outward on x to clear the tire width, and check they still clear the fender too. I'm adjusting the box's z-range further to avoid these collisions.

Now I'm resolving another overlap with the transmission near the box's inner x-edge, so I'll recenter the boxes along z and tweak their length. Then I move on to adding decal planes on the box outer faces (angled chevron graphics facing outward on each side), followed by placing a small chrome gauge cylinder on the handlebar's center clamp, tilted toward the rider with its own face plane for the gauge display.

Next I'm detailing the gauge dial texture (dark circle face with orange ticks), checking that the plane's svg texture gets flagged as coloured for detection purposes, then shaping the headlight as a flattened sphere with a protruding lens cylinder, painted teal with an orange accent strip. I keep a mental tally of part count to stay under budget, then start building the mirror assembly—a chrome stalk rod running from the clutch perch up to a flattened icosahedron mirror head.

Now I'm angling the mirror head backward with a rotation, giving it a faceted chrome front and a slightly smaller, inset dark glass face colored teal-blue. For turn signals I'm skipping the fronts and placing small amber-glowing signal stalks on the rear fender sides. For the chain I'm keeping it simple with dark rods plus small merged boxes spaced along the top run to suggest link bumps.

Now I'm defining the rear sprocket as a cylinder attached to the wheel bone so it spins with the wheel, with a ring of small merged boxes forming teeth, a steel-dark color, and an orange hub plate, plus a smaller front sprocket cylinder on the frame bone. For the engine I'm going with a dark steel body, lighter steel cylinder heads, and orange-painted rocker cover boxes, and I'm starting to lay out the cylinder geometry with direction and base vectors for each cylinder.

Continuing cylinder geometry... adding fins, heads, rocker covers, and chrome pushrod tubes...

Positioning the left primary cover cylinder with its center offset to clear the crankcase width, then adding an inner steel disc detail.

I'm checking that the front cylinder's fin geometry doesn't collide with the air cleaner's position, confirming they stay clear. I'll leave wires and hoses out for now, and I'm adding a frame gusset plate near the head tube by extruding a triangular outline on both sides of the frame.

Now I'm sketching a chrome crash bar guard that loops around the front of the engine, mirrored on both sides, while skipping a separate belly pan for simplicity.

Dropping the symmetric engine guards to avoid clutter, and instead planning a black clutch cable sweeping from the lever down to the engine as a thin detail line.

I'm skipping full brake-line routing since the caliper placement makes it messy, simplifying to just one throttle/clutch cable curve from the right lever down to the carb area. With parts count around 350 I'm also deciding to skip rear shocks since it's a hardtail design.

Now I'm placing the kickstand as a rod between its pivot joint and foot pad position, adding a small mounting bracket on the frame, and working out the license plate bracket position based on where the rear fender curve ends behind the wheel.

I'm placing the tail lamp just outward from the fender surface along its radial direction, positioning it near the fender's curve at roughly θ145 so the glow sits flush against the bodywork rather than floating above it.

I also figure out the plate's placement at θ165, tilting its center slightly to face outward and down along the fender arc, accepting rough overlaps since precision here isn't critical.

Now I'm checking the type imports needed for coloring the part—confirming Paint and Fill types come from the paint and context modules, and that mix and countershade functions handle the Rgb conversion I need for shading.

I'm defining a tone helper that blends the base color toward white and a dark navy for countershading softness, then setting up a seat paint function and moving into the wheel geometry logic—generating spoke rods radiating from the hub to the rim in alternating directions, plus chrome hub flange discs at the axle ends.

Now I'm working through the disc brake and caliper placement on the front wheel bone versus steering, then preparing to build the main body, and laying out my color palette with black, steel tones, chrome, teal, navy, orange, cream, red, and amber for the final paint pass.

I'm writing a helper function to generate rod geometry between two points using a cylinder, then planning out the fender sweep using arc points and box-section sweep options.

I need to make sure the radius function returns a proper tuple type `[number, number]` to avoid typecheck errors, and I'm setting flat caps with fender paint and a bone binding for steering.

Next I'm sweeping the handlebar path with a chrome color and round caps using a numeric radius. Then I'm sketching an SVG dial gauge with a dark background, orange dashed ring, a needle pointer, and a center dot.

Still writing SVG icons...

I'll avoid real logos, using plate text like "CHOP-01" instead, then start writing the full builder function with joint imports, glow effects, and the chopper motorbike structure.

Still writing helper functions...

Now I'm setting up the tank filler and bolt geometry helpers, then writing the final assembly code with careful attention to arithmetic—calling the wheel function for the front wheel with specific radius, tube, rim, and bolt-width parameters, and computing tread outer radius from rim and tube values.

Still placing fork components...

For the headlamp I'm shading the sphere with a teal paint and adding an orange stripe where the top faces upward, keeping the fender details simple with maybe a cream pinstripe. With everything mapped out, I'm ready to write it all, estimating roughly ten parts per wheel assembly between tire, rim, hub, and rings.

Checking the sweep and rod function signatures to make sure tapered radius tuples and chrome colors pass correctly, and confirming the mirrored loop structure for symmetric parts. Skipping extra spike or cushion details, I'm finalizing the code now.
